claim: NFRe is predicted to encode a LysM receptor protein with a typical intracellular kinase domain
source: NFRe is predicted to encode a LysM receptor protein with a typical intracellular kinase domain (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on structural prediction and domain analysis shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The NFRe ectodomain binds M. loti Nod factor with an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 29.1 ± 7.1 μM
source: Affinity measurements showed that the ectodomain of NFRe has the capacity to bind M. loti Nod factor with an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 29.1 ± 7.1 μM (Figure 1B,E).
evidence: Measured by biolayer interferometry experiments with purified NFRe ectodomain and biotinylated Nod factor

claim: NFRe ectodomain does not bind to chitin pentamer (CO5) ligands
source: Next, we tested whether NFRe has the capacity to bind chitin but no signal was observed for CO5 ligands in this system (Figure 1B).
evidence: Biolayer interferometry binding assay showed no detectable signal for CO5

claim: NFR1 ectodomain binds M. loti R7A Nod factor with a KD of 34 ± 6.3 μM
source: To test our immobilised ligands, we performed the same binding experiment with purified NFR1 ectodomain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which gave a KD of 34 ± 6.3 μM to M. loti R7A Nod factor and no binding to CO5 (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: Measured by biolayer interferometry with purified NFR1 ectodomain

claim: Arabidopsis CERK1 ectodomain binds chitin pentamer with an affinity of 59 μM
source: As a positive control for our chitin ligand we additionally expressed and purified the Arabidopsis CERK1 ectodomain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and measured an affinity of 59 μM to the immobilized CO5 (Figure 1D,E), which is very similar to the previously reported KD of 66 μM measured by isothermal titration calorimetry (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Measured by biolayer interferometry and compared to published ITC data

claim: NFRe and NFR1 receptor ectodomains distinguish Nod factor from pentameric chitin ligands in a BLI binding assay
source: In short, our binding studies show that NFRe has the capacity to perceive Nod factor with comparable affinity as seen for the NFR1 and both receptor ectodomains distinguish Nod factor from pentameric chitin ligands in a BLI binding assay (Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on differential binding results from BLI experiments showing binding to Nod factor but not to CO5

claim: NFRe kinase transphosphorylates myelin basic protein (MBP) substrate and autophosphorylates
source: E. coli-produced NFRe kinase transphosphorylated the myelin basic protein (MBP) substrate and autophosphorylated (Figure 1F, lanes 1–3), showing that NFRe encodes a protein kinase with in vitro activity similar to NFR1 (Madsen et al., 2011).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay with radioactive ATP showing phosphorylation of MBP and autophosphorylation

claim: Alanine substitutions of D418, D436, or T459 abolished the phosphorylation activity of NFRe
source: Alanine substitutions of three critical amino acids from the catalytic loop (D418), Mg2 +binding loop (D436), or P+1 loop (T459) abolished the phosphorylation activity of NFRe (Figure 1F, lanes 4–12) showing that conserved residues from NFRe kinase are critical for its biochemical activity.
evidence: In vitro kinase assays with mutant versions showing loss of activity

claim: Nfre encodes a LysM receptor kinase that can perceive Nod factor and has an active kinase
source: Together, our results from biochemical studies demonstrate that Nfre encodes a LysM receptor kinase that can perceive Nod factor and has an active kinase.
evidence: Summary of binding and kinase activity data

claim: nfr1-1 roots transformed with empty vector did not show any responses to inoculation with rhizobia
source: While nfr1-1 roots transformed with the Nfr1 gene developed bona fide root nodules and induced Nin promoter, those transformed with the empty vector, and thus expressing the native Nfre gene did not show any responses to inoculation with rhizobia (Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Complementation experiment showing no nodulation or Nin induction in empty vector controls

claim: Nfre in its native status cannot replace the functions of NFR1
source: These results indicate that Nfre, in its native status cannot replace the functions of NFR1.
evidence: Based on complementation experiments showing no rescue of nfr1-1 phenotype by endogenous Nfre

claim: p35S-Nfre led to strong activation of the Nin promoter after inoculation with M. loti only in the outer root layers
source: On the other hand, p35S-Nfre led to strong activation of the Nin promoter after inoculation with M. loti (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This symbiotic induction was however, only detected in the outer root layers (Figure 2A), and it was not followed by formation of nodules or infection threads even after 5 weeks of exposure to M. loti (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: GUS staining and microscopy showing Nin activation restricted to epidermis

claim: p35S-Nfr1-mediated signalling induced Nin expression in both epidermal and cortical cells and led to formation of infected nodules
source: This differed from the p35S-Nfr1-mediated signalling that induced Nin expression in both epidermal and cortical cells (Figure 2B) and led to formation of infected nodules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: GUS staining showing broader Nin activation and nodule formation with NFR1

claim: Lys2, Cerk6 or Lys7 driven by 35S promoter could not activate the Nin promoter or induce nodule or infection thread formation in the nfr1-1 mutant
source: Under similar conditions, Lys2, Cerk6 or Lys7 driven by 35S promoter could not activate the Nin promoter, or induce nodule or infection thread formation in the nfr1-1 mutant. (Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Complementation experiments with other LysM receptors showing no symbiotic responses

claim: NFRe can initiate a symbiotic signalling cascade leading to Nin induction in Lotus roots in the presence of M. loti
source: These results demonstrate that in the presence of M. loti, NFRe, like NFR1, can initiate a symbiotic signalling cascade leading to Nin induction in Lotus roots, and that the cellular effects of this signalling are receptor-, and expression-dependent.
evidence: Based on differential complementation results with different receptors and promoters

claim: The Nfre promoter is preferentially active in root hair epidermal cells in the susceptible zone of the root and in the root tip in uninoculated roots
source: In uninoculated roots the Nfre promoter (2,6 kb) was preferentially active in root hair epidermal cells, in the susceptible zone of the root, and in the root tip (Figure 2C,E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Promoter-reporter fusion analysis using GUS and tYFPnls

claim: Nfr1 is expressed in the whole uninoculated root
source: This differed from Nfr1 that is expressed in the whole uninoculated root (Radutoiu et al., 2003; Kawaharada et al., 2017) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Promoter-reporter analysis and published data

claim: The expression pattern of Nfre did not change after inoculation with M. loti
source: The expression pattern of Nfre did not change after inoculation with M. loti (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that, unlike Nfr1 (Radutoiu et al., 2003; Kawaharada et al., 2017) and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), the expression of Nfre is not symbiotically regulated.
evidence: Promoter-reporter analysis before and after inoculation

claim: Nfr1 transcript levels are 3-fold higher than Nfre in uninoculated wild type roots
source: Direct comparison of Nfr1 and Nfre transcript levels in uninoculated wild type roots showed a 3-fold higher level for Nfr1.
evidence: Quantitative RT-PCR measurements in uninoculated roots

claim: After Nod factor treatment or M. loti inoculation, Nfr1 expression was down regulated while Nfre maintained a low but constant level
source: Interestingly this difference was reduced significantly after Nod factor treatment (8 hr post treatment) or M. loti inoculation (2 and 3 dpi post inoculation), where Nfr1 expression was down regulated, while Nfre maintained a low, but constant level (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Quantitative RT-PCR measurements after treatments

claim: Nfre and Nfr1 differ in their expression level and pattern in uninoculated roots and follow a differential regulation during root nodule symbiosis
source: In summary, Nfre and Nfr1 differ in their expression level and pattern in uninoculated roots, and follow a differential regulation during root nodule symbiosis.
evidence: Summary of expression pattern and qRT-PCR data

claim: Homozygous nfre mutants formed significantly fewer nodules compared to wild type when grown in binary association with M. loti
source: Homozygous mutant plants from three independent alleles with exonic insertion of LORE1 retroelement (Mun et al., 2016) (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1) formed significantly fewer nodules compared to wild type when grown in a binary association with M. loti (Figure 3A).
evidence: Nodulation phenotyping of three independent mutant alleles

claim: nfre mutants developed only half the number of wild type nodules after 9 weeks growth in soil exposed to native bacterial community
source: The contribution of NFRe to root nodule organogenesis became even more evident when wild type and nfre mutants were grown in soil and were exposed to the native bacterial community. After 9 weeks, nfre mutants developed only half the number of wild type nodules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Nodulation counts in soil-grown plants

claim: The shoot biomass and general plant fitness of nfre mutants were significantly reduced compared to wild type
source: The shoot biomass and the general plant fitness were significantly reduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measurements of shoot fresh weight and plant phenotype observations

claim: nfre mutants had a significantly lower ability to reinitiate nodule formation on the expanding root system at five weeks post inoculation
source: Analyses of the dynamics of nodule primordia formation on plate-grown plants, revealed that nfre mutants, besides a noticeable reduced nodulation at the early time point (two wpi), had a significantly lower ability to reinitiate nodule formation on the expanding root system (five wpi) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Time-course analysis of nodule primordia formation

claim: The formation of infection threads was not affected by mutations in Nfre
source: Unlike nodule organogenesis, the formation of infection threads (IT) appeared not to be affected by mutations in the Nfre. A similar number of ITs were present in wild type and nfre root hairs at 9 or 14 dpi (Figure 3C).
evidence: Quantification of infection threads in wild type and mutants

claim: The mature nodules formed on nfre appeared normally infected
source: The mature nodules formed on nfre appeared normally infected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and the proportion of pink/total nodules formed by soil-grown wild type and nfre plants was similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating a normal infection process in the nfre mutants.
evidence: Microscopic observation and nodule color assessment

claim: The average inter-spike interval of calcium oscillations was significantly longer in nfre cells (106 s) compared to wild type (86 s)
source: Closer inspection of the spiking frequency revealed that the average inter-spike interval was significantly longer in the nfre cells (106 s) compared to wild type (86 s), indicating that NFRe contributes to a constant interval length of calcium oscillations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Calcium imaging analysis using YC3.6 sensor and CaSA software

claim: 44 out of 90 genes differentially expressed by Nod factor in wild type were not regulated in nfre roots
source: A large proportion of these (44 out of 90), which includes Nin, expansins, nodulins, receptors, transporters and transcription factors, were regulated by Nod factor in wild type but not in the nfre roots, indicating that their appropriate regulation in the susceptible zone, at 24 hr after Nod factor treatment is dependent on an active NFRe (Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: RNA sequencing analysis comparing wild type and nfre mutants after Nod factor treatment

claim: Wild type, nfre-1 and nfre-2 mutants produced comparable levels of ROS in response to CO8 or CO4
source: We found that wild type, nfre-1 and nfre-2 mutants produced comparable levels of ROS, indicating that NFRe is unlikely to be involved in chitin signalling (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Chemiluminescent ROS assay with chitin oligomers

claim: NFRe represents an influential component of the epidermal Nod factor signalling in L. japonicus
source: Together, these results show that NFRe represents an influential component of the epidermal Nod factor signalling in L. japonicus, promoting intracellular signalling that leads to optimal calcium spiking, activation of gene transcription and efficient nodule organogenesis on the expanding root system.
evidence: Summary of mutant phenotypes including calcium spiking, transcription, and nodulation defects

claim: The signalling capacity of NeK receptor (NFR1 ectodomain-NFRe kinase) was similar to that of NFRe, inducing only epidermal Nin promoter activation
source: We observed that the signalling capacity of NeK receptor was similar to that of the NFRe, namely only epidermal induction of the Nin promoter (Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Complementation experiment with chimeric receptor showing epidermal-specific Nin induction

claim: A molecular determinant for specific Nin induction is present in the intracellular regions of NFR1 and NFRe receptors
source: This provides evidence for the presence of a molecular determinant for specific Nin induction in the intracellular regions of NFR1 and NFRe receptors.
evidence: Based on chimeric receptor experiments showing kinase domain determines signalling output

claim: NeKA1 (NFR1 ectodomain-NFRe kinase with NFR1 activation segment) led to cortical activation of Nin and nodule formation
source: In contrast to the NeK receptor that induced Nin in the outer root cell layers of the nfr1-1 mutant, NeKA1 led to cortical activation of Nin and nodule formation (Table 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Complementation experiment with chimeric receptor containing swapped activation segment

claim: The activation segment in NFR1 and NFRe determines the downstream signalling output in Lotus roots after M. loti inoculation
source: These results show that the activation segment in NFR1 and NFRe determines the downstream signalling output in Lotus roots after M. loti inoculation.
evidence: Based on differential signalling of chimeric receptors with swapped activation segments

claim: NFR5 is a substrate for the NFRe kinase
source: The in vitro kinase assays showed that NFR5 is a substrate for the NFRe kinase. (Figure 4A, lanes 1–3) and that this transphosphorylation was dependent on the activation segment of the NFRe kinase.
evidence: In vitro kinase assay showing phosphorylation of NFR5 by NFRe

claim: Mutation of T459 to A abolished the kinase activity of NFRe
source: Mutation of T459 to A abolished the kinase activity of NFRe, while exchanging the native segment with the corresponding region of NFR1 maintained transphosphorylation (Figure 4A, lanes 4–6, 7–9).
evidence: In vitro kinase assay with mutant and chimeric kinases

claim: YFP tagged NFRe protein localizes to the plasma membrane
source: The YFP tagged NFRe protein was found to localize to the plasma membrane and to co-localise with the plasma membrane marker, AtPIP2, like previously observed for NFR1 and NFR5 (Madsen et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Confocal microscopy of YFP-tagged protein in N. benthamiana with plasma membrane marker

claim: NFRe forms homomeric complexes alone and heteromeric complexes when co-expressed with either NFR1 or NFR5
source: Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) analyses based on split YFP revealed that NFRe formed homomeric complexes alone and heteromeric complexes when co-expressed with either NFR1 or NFR5 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: BiFC experiments in N. benthamiana showing YFP reconstitution

claim: The formation of heteromeric complex between NFRe and NFR5 was not affected by kinase inactivation
source: The formation of heteromeric complex with NFR5 was not affected by kinase inactivation (Figure 4B).
evidence: BiFC experiments with kinase-dead NFRe mutant

claim: A signalling cascade leading to leaf cell death dependent on an active NFRe kinase was identified in N. benthamiana leaves co-expressing NFRe and NFR5
source: Like in the case of NFR1-NFR5 co-expression (Madsen et al., 2011), a signalling cascade leading to leaf cell death, dependent on an active NFRe kinase, was identified in N. benthamiana leaves co-expressing NFRe and NFR5 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cell death phenotype in N. benthamiana leaves co-expressing receptors

claim: Nfre driven by 35S promoter failed to induce Nin:GUS symbiotic reporter in the nfr5-2 mutant background
source: Finally, we analysed whether the NFRe-dependent activation of Nin in L. japonicus roots was dependent on NFR5. Nfre driven by 35S promoter failed to induce Nin:GUS symbiotic reporter in the nfr5-2 mutant background (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Complementation experiment in nfr5-2 mutant showing no Nin activation

claim: NFRe can interact with and trans-phosphorylates NFR5 kinase and induce a signalling cascade dependent on the NFR5 receptor
source: These results demonstrate that NFRe can interact with, and trans-phosphorylates NFR5 kinase, and induce a signalling cascade dependent on the NFR5 receptor.
evidence: Summary of BiFC, kinase assay, and genetic complementation data

claim: Recognition of Nod factors by LysM receptors is crucial for nitrogen-fixing symbiosis in most legumes
source: Recognition of Nod factors by LysM receptors is crucial for nitrogen-fixing symbiosis in most legumes.
evidence: Established knowledge in the field

claim: Only NFR1 and NFR5 and their closest homologs are known to be required for Nod factor recognition in legumes
source: The large families of LysM receptors in legumes suggest concerted functions, yet only NFR1 and NFR5 and their closest homologs are known to be required.
evidence: Summary of prior knowledge about LysM receptors

claim: Mutants of Nfre react to Nod factors with increased calcium spiking interval
source: Mutants of Nfre react to Nod factors with increased calcium spiking interval, reduced transcriptional response and fewer nodules in the presence of rhizobia.
evidence: Summary of mutant phenotypes from calcium imaging, RNA-seq, and nodulation assays

claim: NFRe has an active kinase capable of phosphorylating NFR5
source: NFRe has an active kinase capable of phosphorylating NFR5, which in turn, controls NFRe downstream signalling.
evidence: In vitro kinase assays and genetic complementation experiments

claim: NFR5 controls NFRe downstream signalling
source: NFRe has an active kinase capable of phosphorylating NFR5, which in turn, controls NFRe downstream signalling.
evidence: Genetic complementation showing NFRe requires NFR5 for signalling

claim: Perception of Nod factors by LysM receptor kinases NFR1 and NFR5 in Lotus japonicus triggers events leading to root nodule symbiosis
source: Perception of Nod factors by LysM receptor kinases, NFR1 and NFR5 in Lotus japonicus (Broghammer et al., 2012), triggers tightly coordinated events leading to root nodule symbiosis (Madsen et al., 2003; Radutoiu et al., 2003).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: Minutes after activation of receptors, a signalling cascade leading to regular calcium oscillations in root hair cells in the susceptible zone is initiated
source: Minutes after the activation of receptors, a signalling cascade (Stracke et al., 2002; Antolín-Llovera et al., 2014) leading to regular calcium oscillations in the root hair cells located in the susceptible zone is initiated (Miwa et al., 2006).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: Calcium oscillations are interpreted by Calcium Calmodulin Kinase (CCaMK)
source: These oscillations are interpreted by the Calcium Calmodulin Kinase (CCaMK) (Miller et al., 2013), which activates a set of regulators that launch transcription of symbiosis specific genes in the outer root cell layers (Yano et al., 2008; Hirsch et al., 2009).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: Mutations in Nfr5 and its homologs in pea and M. truncatula eliminate all Nod factor-induced physiological, molecular and cellular responses
source: Mutations in Nfr5 and its homologs in pea and M. truncatula eliminate all Nod factor-induced physiological, molecular and cellular responses (Madsen et al., 2003; Arrighi et al., 2006).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: Some or several Nod factor responses are retained in the Ljnfr1, Mtlyk3 and Pssym37 mutants
source: However, some or several of these responses are retained in the Ljnfr1, Mtlyk3 and Pssym37 mutants (Radutoiu et al., 2003; Smit et al., 2007; Zhukov et al., 2008) raising the possibility that modular receptor complex formation regulated in a spatio-temporal manner might contribute to Nod factor signalling.
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: The LysM receptor kinase family has greatly expanded in legumes through whole genome or tandem duplications
source: The LysM receptor kinase family has greatly expanded in legumes through whole genome or tandem duplications (Zhang et al., 2009; Lohmann et al., 2010; Kelly et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: In L. japonicus, four genes (Lys1, Lys2, Lys6 and Lys7) are closely related to Nfr1
source: In L. japonicus, four genes, Lys1, Lys2, Lys6 and Lys7, are closely related to Nfr1.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis and established knowledge

claim: Lys1 and Lys2 are located in tandem and at ~10 kb distance from Nfr1
source: Lys1 and Lys2 are located in tandem and at ~10 kb distance from Nfr1 (Lohmann et al., 2010).
evidence: Genomic location information from cited literature

claim: A similar chromosomal organisation of NFR1-type receptors was reported in all studied legumes and in genomes outside of Leguminosae clade
source: Interestingly, a similar chromosomal organisation of NFR1-type receptors was reported in all studied legumes, as well as in genomes outside of Leguminosae clade raising the possibility that gene duplication leading to tandem NFR1-type receptors preceded the evolution of the legume family (De Mita et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparative genomics from cited literature

claim: Only the intracellular kinase regions of LYS6 and LYS7, but not that of LYS2, could restore nodulation and/or infection when coupled to the NFR1 Nod factor-binding domain
source: Nonetheless, key details about the signalling competencies of LYS2, LYS6 and LYS7 were obtained from functional complementation analyses in the nfr1 mutant using the LjUbiquitin promoter. Only the intracellular kinase regions of LYS6 and LYS7, but not that of LYS2, could restore nodulation and/or infection when coupled to the NFR1 Nod factor-binding domain (Nakagawa et al., 2011).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: LYS1 is an epidermal LysM receptor contributing to the NFR1-NFR5 mediated signalling in a spatio-temporal manner
source: Here, we show that LYS1 is an epidermal LysM receptor contributing to the NFR1-NFR5 mediated signalling in a spatio-temporal manner.
evidence: Summary of findings from expression, localization, and functional studies

claim: LYS1 is primarily expressed in epidermal cells of the susceptible zone where roots are competent for initiation of symbiosis
source: This gene is primarily expressed in epidermal cells of the susceptible zone where roots are competent for initiation of symbiosis, and has a restricted signalling capacity leading to Nin activation in the outer root cell layers.
evidence: Promoter-reporter analysis showing tissue-specific expression

claim: LYS1 has a restricted signalling capacity leading to Nin activation in the outer root cell layers
source: This gene is primarily expressed in epidermal cells of the susceptible zone where roots are competent for initiation of symbiosis, and has a restricted signalling capacity leading to Nin activation in the outer root cell layers.
evidence: Complementation experiments showing epidermal-specific Nin induction

claim: LYS1 activity in the outer root cell layers aids in maintaining a normal calcium spiking interval in the root hairs
source: Our findings provide evidence for a complex Nod factor signalling where LYS1 activity in the outer root cell layers aids in maintaining a normal calcium spiking interval in the root hairs, integral transcript responses in the susceptible root zone, and initiation of nodule primordia on the expanding root system.
evidence: Calcium imaging showing altered spiking in mutants

claim: The Lys1 gene is renamed Nfre in accordance with the identified role during Nod factor signalling in the epidermal layer
source: The Lys1 gene is therefore renamed Nfre, in accordance with the identified role of this gene during Nod factor signalling in the epidermal layer.
evidence: Based on functional characterization showing epidermal-specific role

claim: NFRe and NFR1 share similar Nod factor-binding affinity
source: NFRe and NFR1 share biochemical and molecular properties that is similar Nod factor-binding affinity, and chitopentaose differentiating capacity when assessed by biolayer interferometry (Broghammer et al., 2012), functional kinases dependent on fully operative domains (Madsen et al., 2011), capacity to phosphorylate, and induce a signalling cascade dependent of NFR5 (Madsen et al., 2011).
evidence: BLI measurements showing comparable KD values

claim: NFRe and NFR1 have evolved distinct biological properties defined by specific spatio-temporal expression and downstream signalling cascades controlled by diverged kinases
source: In spite of these similarities, NFR1 and NFRe have evolved distinct biological properties defined by specific spatio-temporal expression, and downstream signalling cascades controlled by diverged kinases.
evidence: Summary of expression patterns, complementation results, and chimeric receptor studies

claim: In the absence of the symbiont, Nfre has a low and constant expression in the susceptible zone while Nfr1 outnumbers Nfre in terms of expression level and spatial distribution
source: In the absence of the symbiont, Nfre has a low and constant expression in the susceptible zone, while Nfr1 outnumbers Nfre in terms of expression level and spatial distribution (Figure 4C-1).
evidence: Promoter-reporter analysis and qRT-PCR measurements

claim: Once the symbiotic process is initiated, the expression of NFR1 is rapidly downscaled in the susceptible zone
source: Once the symbiotic process is initiated, the expression of NFR1 is rapidly downscaled in the susceptible zone (Figure 4C-2).
evidence: qRT-PCR measurements after inoculation

claim: A sustained expression of NFRe in the epidermal cells of the susceptible zone could ensure an idling signalling keeping the expanding root system tuned in to rhizobia
source: A sustained expression of NFRe in the epidermal cells of the susceptible zone could ensure an idling signalling, keeping the expanding root system tuned in to rhizobia (Figure 4C-3).
evidence: Based on expression patterns and mutant phenotypes showing reduced nodulation on expanding roots

claim: NFR1 acts as a master switch triggering recurrent symbiotic events in a fast and efficient manner from NFRe-attuned epidermal cells
source: NFR1 acts as a master switch triggering recurrent symbiotic events in a fast and efficient manner from NFRe-attuned epidermal cells (Figure 4C–4).
evidence: Based on differential expression patterns and signalling capacities of the two receptors

claim: Protein-carbohydrate interactions are usually weak and low-affine in the micromolar-millimolar range
source: In general, protein-carbohydrate interactions are usually weak and low-affine (micromolar-millimolar range) (Holgersson et al., 2005) and signalling therefore, emerges as being controlled by ligand multivalency and/or by receptor multiplicity (Kiessling and Pohl, 1996; Rabinovich, 2002; Vasta et al., 2012).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: Studies of receptors at plant and mammalian plasma membrane revealed a conserved strategy to ensure specific signalling via combinatorial systems
source: In line with this notion studies of receptors present at the plant and mammalian plasma membrane revealed a conserved strategy to ensure specific, instantaneous, switchable and evolvable downstream signalling; namely, increased responsiveness and specificity via combinatorial systems (Ostrom et al., 2001; Piñeyro, 2009; Bodmann et al., 2015; Bücherl et al., 2017).
evidence: Established knowledge from cited literature

claim: Multiple LysM receptors may assemble into functional signalling complexes where signalling specificity is the result of the nature of the complex
source: It is possible that multiple LysM receptors assemble into functional signalling complexes where signalling specificity is the result of the nature of the complex, rather than isolated LysM receptors alone.
evidence: Based on BiFC data showing receptor interactions and general knowledge of receptor signalling

claim: Differences might exist among legumes in NFR1-NFRe signalling since nfr1 in Lotus and lyk3 or sym37 in Medicago and pea have different symbiotic phenotypes
source: The mechanistic details of NFR1-NFRe signalling remain to be discovered, but we envision that differences might exist among legumes, since nfr1 in Lotus and lyk3 or sym37 in Medicago and pea have different symbiotic phenotypes (Radutoiu et al., 2003; Smit et al., 2007; Zhukov et al., 2008), indicating distinct evolutionary trajectories after separation of the IRLC (Inverted Repeat-lacking clade) legumes (Sprent, 2008).
evidence: Comparison of mutant phenotypes across species from cited literature

claim: Tandem NFR1-type receptors are found in all legumes and in non-legume species
source: Tandem NFR1-type receptors are found in all legumes and in non-legume species as well (Liang et al., 2013; De Mita et al., 2014).
evidence: Comparative genomics from cited literature
